name: So (Democratic Republic of Congo)
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: 4.1. Gesogo is a language with lexical tone. The alternance of tone on verbal radicals is hidden in the infinitive, but is regularly observed in both affirmative and negative tenses. 4.2. Nominals can be classified into four tone-groups according to the tone of the radical and suffix. 4.3. The tone-pattern of words is maintained in all observed syntactical positions. 4.4. An acute accent (´) marks a high tone, and an unmarked syllable denotes a normal low tone. A circumflex accent (^) indicates a falling tone, and an inverted circumflex accent denotes a rising tone. A mid-tone is a slipped high tone and is marked with a grave accent (`).
new_statements.citation: Harries, Lyndon. 1955. Grammar of Gesogo. Kongo-Overzee 21(5): 420-440.
new_statements.locator: p. 422, 'Tonal Data', §§4.1-4.4 (PDF page 64 of the saved issue scan; verified against the page image)

new_statements.rule_in_words: The language has lexical tone (high, low, falling, rising, and a 'slipped high' mid tone); nouns fall into four tone classes by radical+suffix tone and word tone patterns are stable across syntactic positions. No word stress is described anywhere in the sketch; the only 'accents' are tone diacritics. Stoop 1989 (pp. 130, 132) independently treats the language as H/L tonal with floating tones and says the tone of nominal prefixes could not yet be determined.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. On tone: verbal-radical tone alternance is hidden in the infinitive; vowel length is grammatical, not lexical (§2.5).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tone patterns of nouns and verb forms, elicited from one informant (Pierre Lifenya, chefferie Baluolambi, at Yakusu, Dec. 1954); tone patterns are said to hold in all observed syntactic positions.
new_statements.identity_note: Identity needs adjudication. Harries 1955 describes 'Gesogo (ligesögo)' of the chefferie Baluolambi (chef-lieu Yonange, Yakusu area, south bank of the Congo west of Kisangani to the Lomami) and states on p. 420 'The language is also known as Topoke or Eso'; Stoop 1989 labels his 'sogo' Guthrie C53 and calls it 'le système sogo ou poke' (p. 128) — in Guthrie, C53 is Poke/Topoke while So(ko) of Basoko is C52. Glottolog/hh nevertheless map both Harries 1955 and Stoop 1989 to sode1235 [soc] (EBALL keyword c.52). So the quoted statement may describe Poke/Topoke [pof] = poke1238 rather than So of Basoko; Carrington's 'Baso/Heso' notes (Basoko variety) are the only material here unambiguously from So proper, and they contain no statement. Motingea 2012 (Basoa) is the source that would settle this.

sources.note: 'Phonetic Data' (pp. 420-421: 7 vowels, grammatical vowel length) and 'Tonal Data' (p. 422): lexical tone language; nominals fall into four tone-groups; word tone-pattern maintained in all syntactic positions; H, L, falling, rising and mid ('slipped high') tones marked. The words stress/accent(-as-prominence) never occur; no statement on word stress.
Motingea 2012 is not among the free ILCAA e-publications listed.

sources.citation: Stoop, Henk. 1989. Le connectif du sogo (C53). Annales Aequatoria 10: 117-125.
sources.note: Syntax of the connective only; examples tone-marked (sogo-sud, Lyombo riverain dialect). Nothing on stress. Bibliography cites Stoop 1987 'Vers une grammaire sogo' (unpublished) and Nsimba Bweta 1973 (Topoke mémoire).

sources.citation: Stoop, Henk. 1989. Les préfixes du sogo (C53). Annales Aequatoria 10: 127-140.
sources.note: §1 'Un peu de phonologie', §1.3 p. 130: on contraction of different tones the high (marked ´) generally wins over the unmarked low; an 'unstable' tone (marked `) behaves like low; floating H/B tones replace the prefix tone. p. 132: the tone of the nominal prefixes 'm'est encore impossible à le déterminer'. Nothing on stress.

sources.note: Only tone-marked specimens (noun classes, possessives, demonstratives, verb paradigms, Lord's Prayer 'in Basa') plus a Bolombooki wordlist with the note '(tones controlled)'. No prose on stress or tone.
